summary: This unit teaches you to look after a property's linen so that it lasts: inspect clean linen for faults, decide whether to use, repair or condemn it, make hand and machine repairs, sew on buttons, and turn worn-out linen into useful things such as cleaning cloths. You will also learn to keep records, control stock and work safely and hygienically.

blocks.p: Linen is one of the biggest running costs of a villa, guest house or hotel. Sheets, towels, pillowcases, napkins and uniforms wear out, and a small fault that is not mended grows into a big one. A worker who can spot a fault early, repair it neatly and recycle what cannot be saved keeps the linen stock healthy and saves the property real money. This unit is for HOSPITALITY VILLA/PROPERTIES SERVICES LEVEL 2 trainees.

The unit has three jobs: **inspect** linen after it is laundered and sort it, **repair** what can be saved, and **recycle** what cannot. Each one has a standard: a repair must be neat, strong and the right colour, and recycled linen must never go back to a guest.

Use the right stitch for each repair

Sew straight, secure seams and finish raw edges
Fix simple machine problems safely

Sort: use, repair or condemn
Choose tools and thread

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and group practical tasks in the Centre's linen room. In the practical tasks you inspect and sort a batch of linen, make hand and machine repairs and turn old towels into cleaning cloths. The assessor looks at your safety, the neatness of your stitching and your records.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: When you take photographs for your practical, photograph the linen, your hands and the work area. Do not photograph other trainees' faces unless they agree.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Reason
What it means
rows: Saves money
Mending a loose hem costs a few minutes and a little thread. A new sheet costs far more. Repairing makes linen last longer and delays the cost of buying new stock.
Keeps standards up
Guests expect clean, undamaged linen. A neat repair that is not seen, or linen taken out of use when it is too worn, protects the property's name.
Keeps stock at par
If damaged linen is not mended, the par stock falls and rooms may be short.
Helps the environment
Less linen is thrown away and less is bought. Fewer things go to the dump.
Gives old linen another use
Worn-out towels and sheets become cleaning cloths, laundry bags and dust sheets, so the property buys fewer of these.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Repair
Mend a fault so the item can go back into guest use.
Condemn
Take an item out of guest use for good because it cannot be mended well enough.
Recycle
Use a condemned item again for a different job, such as cleaning cloths.
Par stock
The number of sets of linen needed to run the property normally.
Stock rotation
Using clean linen in turn so every item wears evenly.
Linen
Bed linen, towels, table linen and often staff uniforms and curtains.

ul: **Bed linen**: sheets (flat and fitted), pillowcases, duvet covers. Many are a **polyester-cotton blend**: strong, quick to dry and they crease less than pure cotton.
**Bath linen**: bath towels, hand towels, face cloths and bath mats, usually made of **terry** (cotton with a looped pile that soaks up water).
**Table linen**: tablecloths and napkins, in cotton, linen or blends.
**Uniforms**: chef's jackets, aprons, housekeeping and front-of-house wear.
The **care label** tells you the fibre and how to wash and iron it. Choose thread, needle and iron heat to match the fabric.

blocks.note: In Jamaica's heat and humidity, damp linen quickly grows mildew (black or green spots and a musty smell). Mildewed linen that will not come clean is condemned, and linen must be fully dry before it is stored. Check the store room for damp.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Needles, pins, scissors, a hot iron and a sewing machine are all in one small work area. Most injuries are pricked fingers, cuts and eye strain. Linen can also carry germs and sharp objects. Good habits prevent both.

head: Hazard
Risk
How you prevent it
rows: Needles and pins
Pricks; swallowed needles; needles lost in linen
Keep them in a pincushion or a closed box, never in your mouth or sleeve
Count your needles before and after the work
Pick up a dropped needle at once
Scissors and shears
Cuts
Keep them sharp, which is safer than blunt
Pass scissors closed, with the handles towards the other person
Cut away from your body and your hand
Use fabric scissors only for fabric
Seam ripper and blades
Cuts
Keep the cap on when not in use
Do not rip towards your hand
Sewing machine
Needle through a finger; shock; hair caught
Keep your fingers flat on the fabric, away from the needle
Switch off and unplug before changing the needle or clearing a jam
Tie back long hair; no loose sleeves
Keep the cable off the floor
Iron
Burns; fire
Stand it upright or switch it off and unplug it when you leave
Keep the cable clear
Poor light and long sitting
Eye strain; neck and back pain
Work in good light, with a lamp if needed
Sit at a proper height; take short breaks
Lifting heavy linen bags
Back strain
Bend your knees, keep the bag close to you, and do not lift above your shoulders
Chemicals
Burns; fumes
Wear gloves for stain remover or bleach; read the label and the safety data sheet (SDS); never mix products

ul: **Launder linen before you repair it.** It is cleaner to handle, and you can see the faults and the true colour.

Wear gloves for dirty linen. If you find linen with **blood or other body fluids** while sorting, wear gloves and follow the property's procedure: bag it in a marked bag and have it washed as the rules say. Never shake it out, and never rinse it with bare hands.
Keep clean and dirty linen apart. Do not put repaired linen on the floor.
Wash your hands before and after handling linen.
If you find a needle, pin or sharp object in linen, put it in a closed container for sharps and tell your supervisor.

blocks.note: Check the repair table for needles at the end of every session. A needle left in a sheet can injure a guest or a laundry worker.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The best time to inspect linen is **as it is folded after laundering**. It is clean, dry and under your hands, so every item is seen on its way to the shelf. Never wait until a guest complains.

flow: Work in good light at a clean table
Lay the item flat and look at both sides
Hold sheets and thin cloth up to the light to find holes and thin patches
Check hems, seams, corners, edges and fasteners
Check for stains that remain after laundering
Sort the item into use, repair or condemn
Mark items for repair and put them in the repair basket

head: Item
Faults to look for
rows: Sheets
Holes; thin or worn patches (hold to the light); split seams; loose hems; torn corners; stains; fitted-sheet elastic that has gone slack or torn
Pillowcases
Split seams; torn openings; stains; thin patches; loose stitching
Duvet covers
Split seams; broken zips or missing ties and buttons; holes; stains
Towels
Loose hems; pulled loops; frayed edges; holes; thin or rough areas; fading and staining
Table linen
Burn holes; hem faults; stains; frayed edges
Uniforms
Missing or loose buttons; split seams; hems; torn pockets; zips; stains

head: Decision
When
Examples
rows: Use
No fault, or only a loose thread that you can snip.
A sheet with no faults; a towel with a single pulled loop (snip it level).
Repair
The fault is small and the rest of the item is sound, and the repair will last and cost less than a new item.
A hem that has come loose; a split seam; a small hole; a missing button.
Condemn
Worn thin, many holes, stains that stay after two or more treatments, or the repair would cost more than a new item.
A sheet worn thin with many holes; a pillowcase with a stain that will not go after two treatments.

blocks.note: A pulled loop in a towel is never pulled out: pulling makes a long run of loops come out. Snip the loop level with the towel using small scissors.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.note: If you find the same fault on many new items from one delivery, tell your supervisor so the supplier can be told. Do not repair all of them quietly and say nothing.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Questions to ask before you repair

ul: Is the rest of the fabric sound, or is it worn thin all over? A patch on thin cloth only moves the problem.
Will the repair show or feel rough to a guest on the skin?
Will it last through more washes?
Is it cheaper than buying a new item?

head: Tool
What it is for
rows: Needles
Come in different sizes. Use a medium needle for sheets and towels, a finer one for light fabrics and a stronger one for thick towels.
Thimble
Protects your finger as you push the needle through.
Pins and pincushion
Hold fabric or a patch in place; the pincushion stores them safely.
Fabric scissors
Sharp, used for fabric only; cutting paper blunts them.
Pinking shears
Scissors with zigzag blades: they cut an edge that frays less.
Small scissors or snips
Cut thread ends and pulled loops.
Seam ripper
Takes out stitches without cutting the fabric.
Tape measure
A soft, bendable tape for measuring fabric and hems.
Tailor's chalk or a washable marker
Marks lines on fabric.
Iron and pressing cloth
Press hems and patches flat.

ul: Choose thread to match the **colour** and the **type** of the fabric. A good match makes the repair neat and strong. Use polyester or polyester-cotton thread for most linen, because it is strong and washes well.
If you cannot match the colour exactly, choose a shade slightly darker rather than lighter.
Use a thread that is as strong as the fabric, but not stronger, which can tear the cloth around it.
Cut a length no longer than your arm. Longer thread tangles and weakens.

blocks.h: The parts of a sewing machine

head: Part
What it does
rows: Needle
Carries the upper thread through the fabric. Change it if it is bent, blunt or burred.
Presser foot
Holds the fabric flat against the feed dogs as it is stitched.
Feed dogs
The small metal teeth under the presser foot that move the fabric along.
Needle plate
The metal plate under the needle, with a slot for the feed dogs.
Bobbin and bobbin case
The small spool under the needle plate that holds the lower thread.
Spool pin
Holds the spool of upper thread.
Tension dial and discs
Control how tightly the upper thread is pulled.
Stitch length and stitch selector
Set the length and type of stitch (straight, zigzag, reverse).
Hand wheel
Turned by hand to raise and lower the needle.
Foot pedal
Pressed with the foot to start the machine and control its speed.
Reverse lever or button
Sews backwards to secure the ends of a seam.

blocks.note: Look in the maker's manual for the needle size and thread for each fabric. As a guide, medium needles suit sheets and thin towels, and a heavier needle suits thick towels. Follow the manual and your instructor.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Stitch
What it looks like
What you use it for
rows: Running stitch
A simple in-and-out line of even stitches
Gathering and light sewing; not strong enough for a seam under strain
Back stitch
Each stitch goes back to meet the end of the one before, making a solid line
The strongest hand stitch: mending a split seam
Tacking (basting)
Long, loose stitches
Holding fabric in place for a short time while you sew it properly; taken out afterwards
Hemming (slip stitch)
Small, nearly invisible stitches along a folded edge
Re-stitching a loose hem
Overcast (whip) stitch
Stitches that wrap over a raw edge
Stopping an edge from fraying
Blanket stitch
A looped stitch along the edge
Finishing and strengthening the edge of a blanket

ul: Thread the needle, knot the end of the thread, and start on the wrong side of the fabric, hiding the knot.
Keep stitches **small and even**, and the thread gently tight, not pulled so hard that the cloth puckers.
To finish, make two or three small stitches over the same spot, then cut the thread close. Do not leave a loose end or a knot on the right side.

flow: Launder and check the item; remove any broken stitches with the seam ripper
Press the old fold line flat
Fold the edge back along the old line and pin it
Tack it if needed
Hem stitch along the fold with matching thread, with small even stitches
Fasten off and remove the tacking
Press and check that the hem is straight and even
Turn the item inside out
Trim loose threads, and overcast the raw edges if they fray
Pin the two edges together
Back stitch along the old seam line, starting a little before the split and ending a little after it
Fasten off and press the seam flat

blocks.p: **Darning** means weaving thread back and forth across a small hole so that the hole is filled. It suits small holes, like those in towels, napkins or knits. Work on the wrong side with a darning needle and thread that matches. Sew rows of small stitches across the hole, beyond its edge, and then weave thread over and under the rows at right angles. Keep the weave flat and not too tight.

When a hole is **too large to darn neatly**, put a patch over it. Use a patch cut from the same kind of fabric, or from condemned linen of the same type. **Wash the patch first** so it does not shrink in the next wash and pucker the item.

flow: Trim the ragged edge of the hole into a neat square or oval
Cut a patch larger than the hole by about 2 to 3 cm on every side, with the grain going the same way as the item
Turn the patch edges under about 1 cm and press
Pin the patch over the hole, on the wrong side for a hidden patch
Tack it in place
Hem stitch around the patch with small even stitches
Turn the item over, turn in the hole's edge and hem it to the patch
Remove the tacking, press and check that it lies flat

blocks.note: Do not sew a patch over thin, worn fabric: the cloth around it will tear next time. Use a patch only where the rest of the item is sound.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Match the button to the others in size, colour and style
Mark the spot where the old button was
Thread a needle with double thread and knot it
Start on the wrong side and bring the needle up through one hole
Place a pin or matchstick on top of the button, to leave a little slack
Sew through the holes several times (about six stitches through each pair)
Remove the pin, and wind the thread around the stitches under the button to make a short stalk
Fasten off on the wrong side

ul: Sew the button on **firmly in the same place**. Never close a gap with a safety pin for good, and never use a button of the wrong size from the sewing drawer.
Check the button hole fits the new button before you finish.

**Sides to middle**: when the centre of a sheet is worn but the edges are sound, cut the sheet down the middle, join the two outer edges with a flat seam and hem the new outer edges. It is a way to save a sheet that would be condemned.
**Frayed edge**: overcast or zigzag it, or trim and re-hem.
**Fitted-sheet elastic**: replace slack elastic by hand or machine.
**Zip or ties on a duvet cover**: replace or re-sew.

flow: Switch off and unplug
Put in the right needle for the fabric and check it is straight and sharp
Wind the bobbin evenly, and put it in the bobbin case
Put the spool on the spool pin and thread the machine in the order shown in the manual, with the presser foot **up**
Bring up the bobbin thread and lay both thread ends behind the presser foot
Set the stitch type and length, and the tension
Test on a scrap of the same fabric
Plug in and start slowly

head: Setting
Typical choice for linen repairs
Notes
rows: Stitch type
Straight for seams and hems; zigzag for raw edges and patches
Zigzag stops a raw edge from fraying
Stitch length
About 2.5 to 3 mm for seams; shorter for fine fabric
Too long a stitch pulls apart; too short can damage the cloth
Tension
Set on the middle to start, then adjust on a scrap
Both threads should lock in the middle of the fabric
Speed
Slow and steady
Fast sewing can wander off the line

flow: Pin the pieces together at right angles to the seam
Lower the needle into the fabric at the start
Lower the presser foot
Sew a few stitches forward, then reverse over them
Sew along the seam, guiding the fabric lightly with your fingers flat and away from the needle
At the end, sew a few stitches in reverse to secure it
Lift the needle and the foot and pull the fabric away; cut the threads

ul: To stop a seam coming undone at each end, **sew a few stitches back over the start and over the end** (back-stitching).
Take pins out before they reach the needle: a needle hitting a pin can break and fly.
Do not pull or push the fabric: let the feed dogs move it.

blocks.note: Keep your fingers **flat on the fabric and well away from the needle**. Switch off and **unplug at the wall** before you change a needle, clear a jam or clean under the plate.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Problem
Likely cause
What to do
rows: Upper thread keeps breaking
Wrongly threaded; tension too tight; old or weak thread; blunt needle
Re-thread with the presser foot up; reduce tension; use new thread or needle
Skipped stitches
Bent, blunt or wrong needle; needle put in wrongly
Change the needle
Loops of thread on the underside
Upper thread not seated in the tension discs, or tension too loose
Re-thread with the foot up; adjust tension
Puckered seam
Tension too tight; stitch too short; fabric pulled
Loosen tension; use a longer stitch; let the machine feed the fabric
Fabric not moving
Feed dogs clogged with lint; presser foot up
Unplug; clean under the plate; lower the foot
Machine jams
Thread tangled in the bobbin area
Unplug; remove fabric; cut tangled thread and clean

blocks.note: Clean the lint from the bobbin area and under the needle plate regularly, and oil the machine only as the maker's manual says. Cover it when it is not in use.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Linen that is **condemned** is taken out of guest use for good. It should not be thrown away if it can be used again. Recycling cuts waste and cuts costs.

head: Product
Made from
How
rows: Cleaning cloths and rags
Worn terry towels, thin cotton sheets
Cut into squares or rectangles; hem or zigzag the edges so they do not fray
Dust sheets
Thin or stained sheets
Hem them, to cover furniture during painting or repairs
Laundry bags
Strong sheet fabric
Sew up the sides and a drawstring or ties
Polishing and glass cloths
Soft, thin cotton
Cut up and keep separate from other cloths
Bandage-type bags, pillow stuffing and so on
Offcuts
As the property decides

blocks.h: Making cleaning cloths from condemned towels

flow: Check the towel is clean; if it is not, launder it
Cut off the hems and any worn or thin areas
Mark squares or rectangles, for example 30 cm by 30 cm
Cut along the lines with fabric scissors
Hem or zigzag every cut edge to stop fraying
Mark or dye the cloths a different colour from guest linen
Fold and store them apart from guest linen

ul: Cut edges are **hemmed or zigzagged** so they do not fray. Raw edges shed threads and look untidy.
Mark or dye cleaning cloths so they are **never sent back to guest rooms** or confused with clean linen. For example, dye them a different colour or sew a small coloured stripe.
Use different coloured cloths for different areas, if the property does (for example bathrooms and kitchens), so germs do not spread.
Do not burn or glue edges.

blocks.p: Some properties give condemned or surplus linen to children's homes, churches, shelters or other community groups. Follow the property's policy. Usually the linen is **washed**, checked and the **property's logo or name is removed or cut out** so it is not used under the property's name.

blocks.note: Do not sell condemned linen to guests, send it back to rooms or burn it in an open drum behind the laundry. Burning linen makes smoke and is unsafe.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: Many Jamaican hotels and villas work with community groups and children's homes. Always ask your supervisor before giving anything away, and keep a record of what was given.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Every item that is repaired or condemned is written in a record. Records let the property replace stock before it runs short, track losses and see which items wear out fastest.

head: Record
What it should show
rows: Date
When the item was checked and repaired or condemned
Item and number
What it was and how many
Fault
Hole, split seam, stain, worn thin and so on
Action
Repaired, condemned, recycled into cleaning cloths, given away
Where it came from
Room, floor, department or uniform
Your name or initials
Who did the work
Faults from a new batch
Which supplier and delivery, so it can be reported

blocks.note: Condemned linen is written in the record book before it is recycled. This lets the property replace stock and track losses. Never recycle or give away linen that has not been recorded.
blocks.label: Remember

ul: **Par stock** is the number of sets of linen needed to run the property normally, including linen in use, in the wash and on the shelf.

**Stock rotation**: use clean linen in turn, with the oldest on top of or in front of the newer stock. **First in, first out (FIFO)** means the linen put on the shelf first is used first. This makes the stock wear evenly.
Count linen regularly (a stock-take) and compare it with the records. Report missing or condemned items so they can be replaced.
Repair costs less than replacing, but an item that would cost more to mend than to replace is condemned.

head: Check
A good repair has
rows: Stitches
Even, small stitches in a straight line
Thread
Matching colour and type
Ends
No loose ends and no knots on the right side
Strength
Secure ends; the item does not pull apart when you tug it gently
Appearance
Flat, with no puckering; the item is pressed
Comfort
Nothing rough or hard that a guest could feel on the skin

ul: After a repair, the item is **checked, pressed and put on a clean shelf**.
Never put a repaired item straight on a guest's bed without a check, and never store linen on the floor or in a plastic bag where damp can build up.
Fold repaired items so the repair is hidden but can be found at the next check.
Tell your supervisor about repeated faults, a delivery of faulty linen, mildew in the store, or a broken machine.
Keep your repair area tidy and the sewing kit complete, and report low stock of thread, needles and buttons.
I can explain why a property repairs and recycles linen, and give three reasons.
I can work safely with needles, pins, scissors, the iron and the sewing machine.
I can handle linen hygienically, including stained and soiled items.
I can inspect linen as it is folded and find holes, thin patches, loose hems, split seams and stains.
I can sort linen into use, repair and condemn, and say why.
I can name the sewing tools and the parts of a sewing machine and say what each does.
I can choose thread, needle and patch to match the job.
I can sew running, back, tacking, hemming and overcast stitches and say when to use each.
I can re-stitch a hem, mend a split seam, darn a small hole and sew on a patch.
I can sew a flat button on firmly.
I can thread a sewing machine, choose the stitch and tension and sew a secure seam.
I can fix simple sewing machine problems safely.
I can turn condemned towels into hemmed cleaning cloths and keep them apart from guest linen.
I can keep records of repaired and condemned linen and explain par stock and FIFO.
I can check a repair before the item goes back to the shelf.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step. For example: 'I wash the patch before sewing it on, so that it does not shrink in the next wash and pucker the item.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: Mending a fault so an item can go back into use.
Taking an item out of guest use for good.
Using worn linen again for another job.
The sets of linen needed to run normally.
First in, first out: using the oldest stock first.
Looped cotton fabric used for towels.
The folded and stitched edge of a sheet or towel.
The woven side edge of fabric that does not fray.
The line of stitches joining two pieces of fabric.
A tool for removing stitches without cutting the fabric.
Scissors with zigzag blades that give an edge that frays less.
The strongest hand stitch, used on split seams.
Long temporary stitches that hold fabric in place.
A small, nearly hidden stitch for a folded edge.
A looped stitch used on the edge of a blanket.
Weaving thread over a small hole to fill it.
A piece of fabric sewn over a hole too large to darn.
The small spool of lower thread under the needle plate.
The part that holds the fabric flat as it is stitched.
The metal teeth that move the fabric along.
How tightly the machine pulls the thread.
The wheel turned by hand to raise and lower the needle.
A machine stitch that stops a raw edge fraying.
Safety data sheet, which comes with a chemical.

c1.title: Inspecting the pile at a Mandeville guest house
c1.text: Trainee Rochelle is folding laundered linen at a guest house in Mandeville. She finds a duvet cover with a seam split open for 20 cm near the zip, a bath mat with a frayed edge, a fitted sheet with one torn corner and loose elastic, and a cotton tablecloth with a burn hole as big as a coin in the middle. All the cloth around the faults is strong and the colours are good. The store keeper wants the repairs done before Friday.

c2.title: A split pillowcase seam in Black River
c2.text: A pillowcase from a Black River villa has a seam that has split for about 15 cm along one side. The fabric is a white polyester-cotton blend and is still strong. Trainee Marlon will mend it by hand. He finds a reel of white polyester-cotton thread, a reel of bright blue cotton and a needle, and he wants the repair to survive many washes.

c3.title: Trouble at the sewing machine in Kingston
c3.text: In a Kingston hotel's linen room, trainee Tanisha is machine-hemming a sheet. The upper thread keeps snapping and the stitches skip. The needle looks slightly bent. She has just threaded the machine with the presser foot down, and she wants to change the needle quickly. A customer-service officer is waiting for the finished sheet.

c4.title: Cleaning cloths from old towels in Ocho Rios
c4.text: A resort in Ocho Rios has 40 condemned bath towels. The housekeeping supervisor asks trainee Devon to cut them into cleaning cloths for the staff. Devon cuts and stacks squares and puts them on the shelf with the clean guest hand towels. The supervisor also asks him to give 20 worn sheets to a local children's home.

c5.title: Stock and records at a Port Antonio villa
c5.text: A villa in Port Antonio keeps 3 sets of bed linen for each of its 6 beds. Trainee Keisha is doing the monthly stock check. Of the 18 sets, 2 sets of sheets are condemned. A new batch of 40 pillowcases arrived last week, and she notices that the seams on 12 of them are already loosening. Her supervisor wants to know what she will do.

c6.title: A needle in the laundry
c6.text: While sorting a heap of laundered sheets, trainee Andre finds a sewing needle pushed through the corner of a sheet. He also finds a pillowcase marked with dried blood. His hands are bare, and the repair table is crowded and poorly lit.

questions.q: Which of Rochelle's items is the best candidate for repair rather than condemning?
o: The duvet cover with the split seam
A sheet worn thin all over
A pillowcase with a stain that stays
A towel with many holes
questions.why: A split seam on a sound duvet cover is a quick, cheap repair. Items worn thin all over or marked with a permanent stain are condemned.

questions.q: What is the best repair for the burn hole in the tablecloth?
o: Leave it, as the guests will not notice it under the plates
Sew a patch of matching fabric over the damaged area
Cut the tablecloth in half and use it as two napkins
Sew the sides of the hole together with a long stitch
questions.why: A hole too big to darn is patched, using sound matching fabric that has been washed first. The cloth around the hole is strong, so a patch will hold.

questions.q: How should Rochelle deal with the frayed edge of the bath mat?
o: Pull the loose threads out until the edge is clean
Burn the loose threads with a flame to seal the edge
Zigzag stitch over the edge, or trim and re-hem it
Glue the edge down with a strong glue
questions.why: A zigzag stitch or a new hem stops the edge fraying. Pulling threads makes more run out, and burning or gluing leaves a hard, unsafe edge.

questions.q: Why is the best time to find these faults when the linen is folded after laundering?
o: Linen is easier to repair when it is wet
Guests are not around to see the faults then
It is cheaper to inspect it at the year-end stock count
It is clean, dry and in the hands, so every item is seen
questions.why: Checking as you fold means every item is looked at on its way to the shelf, before it can fail on a guest's bed. Waiting for a complaint or a yearly count lets small faults grow.

questions.q: Which hand stitch should Marlon use to mend the split seam?
o: Back stitch
Running stitch
Tacking stitch
Blanket stitch
questions.why: Back stitch makes a solid line and is the strongest hand stitch for a seam. Running stitch is not strong enough under strain, tacking is temporary and blanket stitch is for edges.

questions.q: Which thread should Marlon choose?
o: The bright blue cotton, so the repair can be seen
The white polyester-cotton thread, to match the pillowcase
The blue cotton, as it is the strongest thread
No thread, but strong tape stuck over the seam
questions.why: Thread should match the fabric in colour and type, so the repair is neat and lasts through many washes. A contrasting thread would show and a different fibre may wear differently.

questions.q: How should Marlon finish the repair?
o: Leave a long knot on the right side so it can be found later
Pull the thread very tight so the seam closes up firmly
Cut the thread and leave it, as the wash will tighten it
Make a few stitches over the same spot and cut the thread close
questions.why: A few stitches over the same place secure the end without a knot or a loose tail on the right side. Pulling the thread tight puckers the seam.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of the broken thread and skipped stitches?
o: A bent needle, and threading with the foot down
A sheet that is too clean to be sewn
A sheet that is too large for the machine
A hand wheel turned the wrong way
questions.why: Threading with the foot down stops the thread seating in the tension discs, and a bent needle skips stitches. Re-thread with the foot up and change the needle.

questions.q: Before Tanisha changes the needle, what must she do?
o: Run the machine fast to clear the thread
Put a drop of oil on the bent needle
Switch off and unplug it at the wall
Hold the fabric down with her fingers under the foot
questions.why: A machine that is plugged in can start by accident. Always switch off and unplug before changing a needle or clearing a jam.

questions.q: The finished hem is puckered. What is the most likely cause?
o: The needle is too sharp
The tension is too tight, or the fabric was pulled
The hem is too wide to be sewn on a machine
The hem was ironed before it was sewn
questions.why: Tight tension or pulling the cloth through gathers it. Loosen the tension and let the feed dogs move the fabric.

questions.q: While she sews, where should Tanisha keep her fingers?
o: Under the presser foot to guide the cloth
Behind the needle to hold the thread
Flat on the fabric, well away from the needle
Close to the needle, to stop the cloth slipping
questions.why: Fingers flat on the fabric and well away from the needle prevent the needle going through a finger. Let the machine feed the fabric.

questions.q: What should Devon have done with the cut cloths before storing them?
o: Hemmed the edges and marked the cloths as separate
Burned the edges lightly so they would not fray
Left the edges raw so they soak up more water
Folded them with the guest hand towels for easy finding
questions.why: Cut edges are hemmed or zigzagged so they do not fray. Cloths are marked or dyed and stored apart so they never go back to a guest.

questions.q: Why is it a problem to store the cleaning cloths with the guest hand towels?
o: They might be used in a guest room by mistake
They will make the hand towels shrink
They will take up too much room on the shelf
They will wear out the hand towels faster
questions.why: Condemned linen made into cleaning cloths must never be sent back to guest rooms. Marking them and storing them apart prevents mistakes.

questions.q: Before the 20 worn sheets are given to the children's home, what is usually done?
o: They are sprayed with perfume so they smell fresh
They are washed, and the property's logo is removed
They are ironed and wrapped as gifts for guests
They are sewn with new labels showing today's date
questions.why: Linen given away is washed and checked, and the property's name or logo is removed so it is not used under the property's name. Check the property's policy and record what was given.

questions.q: How many sets of linen should the villa have at par stock, and how many does it now have in good condition?
o: Par is 6 sets, and 4 are good
Par is 18 sets, and 16 are good
Par is 18 sets, and 14 are good
Par is 3 sets, and 1 is good
questions.why: 3 sets for each of 6 beds is a par stock of 18. With 2 sets condemned, 16 are in good condition, so the villa is short of par and should replace stock.

questions.q: What should Keisha do about the loose seams on the 12 new pillowcases?
o: Repair them quietly and say nothing, so the supplier is not annoyed
Throw them away before anybody sees
Use them until they split and replace them later
Tell the supervisor so the supplier can be told, and record the fault
questions.why: The same fault on many new items points to a supplier problem. Report it and record it so the property can claim, rather than paying for repairs itself.

questions.q: What must be recorded when the 2 sets of sheets are condemned?
o: Only the number of sheets, as the reason is not needed
The date, items, fault, action and who decided
The price the property paid for each set, and no more
The names of the guests who used them last
questions.why: Records show the date, the items, the fault, the action and who made the decision. They let the property replace stock and track losses.

questions.q: What should Andre do about the needle he found in the sheet?
o: Pull it out with bare fingers and put it in his pocket
Leave it in and take the sheet to the repair table
Put it in a closed sharps container and tell his supervisor
Push it back into the sheet corner so that it is not lost
questions.why: A loose needle can injure a guest or a worker. Handle it carefully, put it in a closed sharps container and report it.

questions.q: How should Andre deal with the blood-stained pillowcase?
o: Rinse it under the tap with his bare hands
Shake it out to see how much blood is on it
Put it with the normal linen to be repaired
Wear gloves and follow the soiled-linen procedure
questions.why: Blood can carry germs. Wear gloves, do not shake it, and bag it and have it washed as the property's procedure says.

questions.q: Why does the poor lighting at the repair table matter?
o: It makes the sewing machine use more power
Small faults and thin patches are hard to see, and eyes tire
It lets guests see the repairs being done more easily
It makes the linen room too warm for work in hot weather
questions.why: Good light shows small holes, thin patches and stitches and protects your eyes. Hold thin cloth up to the light when you inspect it.
